column2: go out of your comfort zone
column7: ɡəʊ aʊt ɒv jɔː ˈkʌmfət zəʊn
column9: To do something unfamiliar or challenging that pushes personal boundaries.
column10: Moving to a new country really forced me to go out of my comfort zone.
column11: You need to go out of your comfort zone if you want to grow.
column12: It was scary, but going out of my comfort zone was the best decision I ever made.

column9: To be taken away quickly and suddenly, often to a pleasant destination.
column10: She was whisked away on a surprise holiday to Italy.
column11: The winner was whisked away for a private interview.
column12: He whisked her away for a romantic weekend.

column9: Something that is very easy or effortless (often used in the negative).
column10: Learning a new language is not a walk in the park.
column11: The exam was a walk in the park for him.
column12: Don't expect this project to be a walk in the park.

column2: let the cat out of the bag
column7: lɛt ðə kæt aʊt ɒv ðə bæɡ
column9: To accidentally reveal a secret.
column10: He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.
column11: Don't let the cat out of the bag before we are ready.
column12: I think I accidentally let the cat out of the bag.

column2: When in Rome, do as the Romans do
column7: wɛn ɪn rəʊm duː æz ðə ˈrəʊmənz duː
column9: Adapt to the customs of the place you are visiting.
column10: I don't usually take afternoon naps, but when in Rome...
column11: She tried eating snails in France; when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
column12: It's best to follow local etiquette—when in Rome, do as the Romans do.

column9: Unimpressed or indifferent to something because one has experienced or seen it so often before.
column10: I was a bit blasé about the whole thing.
column11: He is very blasé about his achievements.
column12: Don't be so blasé about your safety.

column9: Extremely alarming, frightening, or exciting.
column10: The drive along the cliffside was a hair-raising experience.
column11: It was a hair-raising moment when the brakes failed.
column12: She told a hair-raising story about her escape.

column9: A physical reaction where the skin becomes rough with small bumps due to cold, fear, or excitement.
column10: The song was so beautiful that I got goosebumps.
column11: Just thinking about it gives me goosebumps.
column12: He had goosebumps on his arms from the cold wind.

column2: hairs on the back of your neck stand up
column7: hɛəz ɒn ðə bæk ɒv jɔː nɛk stænd ʌp
column9: To feel very scared, uneasy, or sensed danger.
column10: I heard a strange noise, and the hairs on the back of my neck stood up.
column11: The atmosphere in the room made the hairs on the back of my neck stand up.
column12: It was a creepy place that made the hairs on the back of my neck stand up.

column9: Causing extreme fear.
column10: Getting lost in the mountains was an absolutely terrifying experience.
column11: It was a terrifying ordeal for the family.
column12: The noise was absolutely terrifying.

column9: Used to express a fervent wish that something does not happen.
column10: If something were to happen, God forbid, we need to be prepared.
column11: God forbid that we should ever have to go through that again.
column12: I hope, God forbid, you never have to experience this.

column9: To bring bad luck by talking about something good before it happens.
column10: You would jinx it if you said everything was going well before the exam.
column11: Don't say we've won yet; you'll jinx it!
column12: I don't want to jinx my chances by celebrating too early.

column9: To take unnecessary risks or act in a way that invites bad luck.
column10: You wouldn't want to tempt fate by driving without a seatbelt.
column11: Leaving your door unlocked is just tempting fate.
column12: She felt she was tempting fate by booking the holiday before getting the time off.

column9: A word with strong emotional or political connotations beyond its literal meaning.
column10: 'Fear' is a loaded word in this context.
column11: He used a loaded word that upset everyone.
column12: Politicians often use loaded words to sway opinion.

column9: To appear or become visible in a particular way (of a feeling or quality).
column10: Fear could manifest itself in all sorts of forms.
column11: The illness first manifested itself as a severe headache.
column12: Stress often manifests itself physically.

column9: The influence from members of one's peer group.
column10: Teenagers often face peer pressure to fit in.
column11: She resisted the peer pressure to drink alcohol.
column12: Peer pressure can be positive or negative.

column9: To minimize the significance or importance of something.
column10: You can't play down the importance of English in the modern world.
column11: He tried to play down the seriousness of the accident.
column12: The government played down the reports of a crisis.

column2: thrown in at the deep end
column7: θrəʊn ɪn æt ðə diːp ɛnd
column9: To be put into a difficult or challenging situation without preparation or assistance.
column10: I was thrown in at the deep end with my new job.
column11: New teachers are often thrown in at the deep end.
column12: It's a sink or swim situation; you're thrown in at the deep end.

column9: To fail or succeed entirely by one's own efforts.
column10: It's a sink or swim situation in this competitive market.
column11: They gave him no training; it was sink or swim.
column12: You have to learn fast or you'll sink or swim.

column9: To be overwhelmed by a large amount of something (metaphorical).
column10: I felt like I was drowning in work.
column11: She is drowning in debt.
column12: They were drowning in paperwork.

column9: To recall something clearly and vividly.
column10: I remember that distinctly.
column11: He distinctly remembers locking the door.
column12: I remember distinctly what she was wearing.

column9: Unexpectedly revealing or enlightening.
column10: It was an eye-opening moment for me.
column11: The documentary was a truly eye-opening experience.
column12: Traveling to India was eye-opening.

column9: A shocking event that changes the way you think or behave.
column10: The health scare was a wake-up call for him to change his diet.
column11: Failing the exam was a wake-up call.
column12: We need a wake-up call to address climate change.

column9: An occasion that forces you to consider the facts of a situation as they really are.
column10: It was a reality check when I realized how much money I had wasted.
column11: The loss was a reality check for the team.
column12: He needs a reality check if he thinks this will be easy.

column9: Suffering or hard work is necessary in order to achieve something.
column10: It's a tough journey, but remember: no pain, no gain.
column11: The workout was brutal, but no pain, no gain!
column12: He believes in the philosophy of no pain, no gain.

column9: To start something with great energy and immediate success.
column10: You hit the ground running with your new project.
column11: She wants to hit the ground running in her new role.
column12: We need someone who can hit the ground running.

column9: To make a determined effort to deal with a difficult problem or situation.
column10: You tackle their grammatical errors head-on.
column11: We need to tackle the issue of unemployment.
column12: He tackled the problem with enthusiasm.

column9: Feelings of worry or anxiety.
column10: There was a lot of anxiety and nerves before the show.
column11: She suffers from nerves before exams.
column12: I took a deep breath to steady my nerves.

column9: A nervous feeling in one's stomach.
column10: You get butterflies in your stomach before the lesson starts.
column11: I always have butterflies in my stomach before a first date.
column12: The interview gave me butterflies in my stomach.

column9: A situation requiring careful balance and control, often risky.
column10: It's like a tightrope walk, balancing work and family.
column11: Managing the budget is a bit of a tightrope walk.
column12: Diplomacy is often a tightrope walk.

column9: To be moving around loosely or chaotically (often used for thoughts).
column10: You've got all these methods rattling around in your brain.
column11: There's just one idea rattling around in my head.
column12: I heard something rattling around in the box.

column9: To fulfill expectations or standards.
column10: You feel like 'I'm not living up to what they think I should be'.
column11: He found it hard to live up to his parents' expectations.
column12: The film didn't live up to the hype.

column9: Sitting or standing with a drooping, awkward posture.
column10: I remember being slouched and hunched over from exhaustion.
column11: Don't sit slouched in your chair.
column12: He walked with a slouched posture.

column9: The instinctive physiological response to a threatening situation.
column10: It's a fight or flight mechanism triggered by stress.
column11: My fight or flight response kicked in immediately.
column12: Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight.

column9: Ready to face and endure danger or pain; showing courage.
column10: You have to be brave in these situations.
column11: It was a brave decision to quit his job.
column12: She put on a brave face despite the pain.

column9: To succeed in dealing with (a problem or difficulty).
column10: To face your fears and overcome them is a great achievement.
column11: She overcame many obstacles to get here.
column12: He struggled to overcome his shyness.

column9: Without being affected by; despite.
column10: Bravery is acting in spite of your fears.
column11: He went out in spite of the rain.
column12: In spite of the difficulties, we succeeded.

column9: Showing smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements.
column10: Now I'm starting to feel complacent about my progress.
column11: We cannot afford to be complacent about safety.
column12: Success can make you complacent.

column9: Completely relaxed and in control of one's emotions.
column10: It's preferable to be cool, calm and collected during a crisis.
column11: She remained cool, calm and collected throughout the interview.
column12: He tried to appear cool, calm and collected.

column9: Unable to act in a relaxed and natural way because of self-consciousness.
column10: I was inhibited by nerves and couldn't speak.
column11: She felt inhibited by the presence of strangers.
column12: Alcohol makes people feel less inhibited.

column9: A situation where one has to learn a lot in a short period.
column10: It's a steep learning curve when you start a new business.
column11: The new software has a steep learning curve.
column12: She faced a steep learning curve in her first year.

column9: To anticipate with great apprehension or fear.
column10: I used to dread those observed lessons.
column11: She dreads going to the dentist.
column12: I dread to think what might happen.

column9: Causing disgust or distaste.
column10: A slithery snake is repellant to many people.
column11: I found his attitude repellant.
column12: The smell was absolutely repellant.

column9: Feeling or showing caution about possible dangers or problems.
column10: We instinctively know we should be wary of snakes.
column11: Be wary of strangers offering gifts.
column12: Investors are wary of the volatile market.

column9: To try to gain favor by flattering or acting submissively (a stress response).
column10: The 'fawn' response involves trying to please the aggressor.
column11: He fawned over the boss to get a promotion.
column12: Stop fawning and just do your job.

column9: Very great in amount; very strong (emotionally).
column10: The pressure becomes overwhelming.
column11: The response was overwhelming.
column12: She felt an overwhelming sadness.

column9: A hierarchy of status seen among members of a group of people or animals.
column10: In the pecking order, pedestrians are at the bottom.
column11: He is low down in the pecking order at work.
column12: It's important to understand the office pecking order.

column9: Characterized by abrupt stops and starts.
column10: Don't make any jerky movements that might startle someone.
column11: The car made a jerky stop.
column12: His movements were jerky and nervous.

column9: To summon the bravery to do something.
column10: Plucking up the courage to step into the road took a while.
column11: It took him months to pluck up the courage to ask her out.
column12: I finally plucked up the courage to quit.

column9: The legal right of a pedestrian or vehicle to proceed with precedence over others.
column10: The larger vehicles have the right of way.
column11: You must yield the right of way to pedestrians.
column12: Who has the right of way at this junction?

column9: A situation that looks confused but functions effectively.
column10: Traffic in Vietnam is organised chaos.
column11: My desk looks messy, but it's organised chaos; I know where everything is.
column12: The event was a bit of organised chaos.

column2: stick out like a sore thumb
column7: stɪk aʊt laɪk ə sɔː θʌm
column9: To be obviously different from the surrounding people or things.
column10: You're sticking out like a sore thumb in that outfit.
column11: As a foreigner, I stuck out like a sore thumb.
column12: The new building sticks out like a sore thumb.

column9: A person who feels uncomfortable because they are in an unfamiliar environment.
column10: I felt like a fish out of water at the fancy party.
column11: He was a fish out of water in the city.
column12: Without his tools, he was a fish out of water.

column9: To look or seem the same as surrounding people or things and therefore not be easily noticeable.
column10: You try to blend in with the locals.
column11: The chameleon blends in with its background.
column12: She tried to blend in at the back of the room.

column9: To be relaxed and accept a situation rather than trying to control or change it.
column10: You've got to try to go with the flow when traveling.
column11: I just decided to go with the flow and see what happens.
column12: He's very easy-going; he just goes with the flow.
